stem: A linked list gives up O(1) indexing in exchange for:
options: O(1) insertion at a KNOWN position - re-point two arrows, nothing shuffles
explanation: An array's contiguity gives index maths but forces shuffles; scattered nodes give cheap splicing but demand walking.

stem: AddFirst on a singly linked list is O(1) because:
options: New node points at old head; head points at new node - TWO writes, regardless of length
explanation: The same operation on a List<T> shuffles every element right - O(n). This asymmetry is the whole comparison table.

stem: Keeping a _tail reference makes which operation O(1)?
options: AddLast - without it you would walk the whole chain to find the end
explanation: One extra field, constant-time appends. Note RemoveLast stays O(n) on a SINGLY linked list - the tail cannot see backwards.

stem: Removing a node from a singly linked list requires tracking 'previous' because:
options: You bypass the node by pointing PREVIOUS.Next past it - and a node cannot see backwards
explanation: previous.Next = current.Next splices it out. Head removal is the special case with no previous - where linked-list bugs live.

stem: In the one-pass Reverse, why save 'next = current.Next' BEFORE re-pointing?
options: Turning the arrow around DESTROYS the only route to the rest of the chain - save it first
explanation: Remember where you were going, turn the arrow, advance both pointers. Miss step 1 and the tail is garbage-collected mid-walk.

stem: Reversing a singly linked list in one pass costs:
options: O(n) time, O(1) SPACE - three pointers, no copies
explanation: previous/current/next walk once, re-pointing as they go. THE pointer-manipulation exercise, hence its interview fame.

stem: A doubly linked list buys O(1) RemoveLast and backwards walking by paying:
options: One extra pointer per node and DOUBLE the wiring to keep consistent
explanation: Previous pointers must be maintained in every operation. Browser back/forward history is the canonical use.

stem: In practice List<T> usually beats LinkedList<T> even at insertion-heavy work because:
options: CPU CACHES love contiguous arrays - chasing scattered pointers stalls modern hardware
explanation: The theory table lies about constants. You study linked lists because the NODE-AND-POINTER idea builds trees and graphs.

stem: If the only head reference is overwritten without saving it:
options: The ENTIRE chain becomes unreachable and is garbage-collected
explanation: Reachability is everything (4.8): nodes hold each other, but nothing holds the first one. One careless assignment, whole list gone.

stem: Ten lines of GetEnumerator with yield gave the hand-built list:
options: foreach AND all of LINQ - Where, Sum, the lot (3.5's interface)
explanation: Implement IEnumerable<T> once and your type joins the entire ecosystem - the same move as Playlist in 3.5.
